15.title: 1. Environment variables and secrets in production

blocks.text: A secret is anything that costs money or leaks data if someone else has it: API keys, database passwords, access codes. Config is everything else (model name, chunk size, folder paths). Both should live outside your code, so the same code runs on your laptop and in production with different values.

rows: Set in the dashboard of Render, Railway or Streamlit
No keys in source, notebooks or README

blocks.text: Example: fail fast if a variable is missing

import os

def require_env(name):
    value = os.environ.get(name)
    if not value:
        raise RuntimeError(f'Missing environment variable: {name}')
    return value

OPENAI_API_KEY = require_env('OPENAI_API_KEY')
VECTOR_DIR = os.environ.get('VECTOR_DIR', './db')   # config with a default
.gitignore and.env.example:

# .gitignore
.env
.streamlit/secrets.toml
db/

# .env.example (safe to commit)
OPENAI_API_KEY=your-key-here
DEMO_ACCESS_KEY=choose-a-passcode
VECTOR_DIR=./db
Why this matters in practice

items: Git remembers everything. Deleting a key in a later commit does not remove it from history. If a key was ever pushed, treat it as leaked: revoke it at the provider and create a new one.
Bots scan public GitHub repos for keys within minutes.
Failing at startup with a clear message is better than failing on the first user request.
Use a separate key for development and production, so you can revoke one without breaking the other.

blocks.text: Real use case: a student pushes a notebook with OPENAI_API_KEY = 'sk-...' to a public repo. Within hours the account shows thousands of dollars of usage. The fix is to revoke the key, rotate it, and load the new one from the environment.

15.title: 2. Never shipping API keys to the client

blocks.text: The client is anything running on the user's device: browser JavaScript, a mobile app, a desktop app. Anything sent to the client can be read by the user, even if it is hidden in minified code or an environment variable.
The safe pattern: put your own backend in the middle.
Browser / app  --->  Your backend (holds the key)  --->  LLM provider
Your backend adds the key, checks who is calling, applies limits, and returns only the answer.
Example: a minimal FastAPI proxy
Common ways keys leak to the client

items: Calling the provider directly from frontend JavaScript.
Frontend variables that get bundled into the public build (for example names starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_ or VITE_).
Keys inside a mobile app package, which can be unpacked.
Returning the full request, headers or an error object from your API.

blocks.text: Note on Streamlit: a Streamlit app runs its Python on the server, so a key in st.secrets is not sent to the browser. The danger is printing it, or showing raw exceptions on the page.

Why this matters in practice: a key in the client is public. Anyone can copy it and run up your bill. Your backend is also the right place to add authentication, rate limits and logging (sections 7 to 9).

Real use case: a React chat widget needs GPT answers. Instead of calling OpenAI from the browser, it calls /chat on your FastAPI service, which checks a passcode, applies a daily limit and then calls the model.

15.title: 3. Deploying a Streamlit app to Streamlit Community Cloud

blocks.text: Streamlit Community Cloud runs your app straight from a GitHub repo. Push to the repo and the app redeploys.
Steps
1. Put app.py and requirements.txt in a GitHub repo (see section 5).
2. Make sure.env and.streamlit/secrets.toml are in.gitignore.
3. Sign in at share.streamlit.io with GitHub and choose Create app.
4. Pick the repo, branch and main file (for example app.py).
5. Open Advanced settings: choose the Python version and paste your secrets.
6. Deploy, then open the logs if anything fails (section 10).
Secrets format. Paste this in the Secrets box (it is TOML). For local testing, put the same text in.streamlit/secrets.toml, which must never be committed.

OPENAI_API_KEY = 'sk-your-key'
APP_PASSWORD = 'choose-a-passcode'
Reading secrets in code (works on the cloud and locally):
Things to know

items: The disk is temporary. Files written at runtime (a Chroma folder, uploads) can disappear when the app restarts or sleeps (section 6).
Free apps go to sleep after a period of no visitors and take a moment to wake up.
Resources (memory, CPU) are limited, so avoid loading large local models.
Limits, sharing options and private-repo rules change, so check the current Streamlit docs.

blocks.text: Real use case: a 'chat with the HR policy PDF' demo for a portfolio. The repo holds the code and a small data/ folder, the secrets hold the API key and a passcode, and the README links to the live URL.

15.title: 4. Deploying a Flask or FastAPI service to Render or Railway

blocks.text: Both platforms build your repo, run one start command, and give you a public URL. The details that cause most failures are the same on both.
The three rules
1. Listen on the port the platform gives you. Read the PORT environment variable.
2. Bind to 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1, or the platform cannot reach your app.
3. Use a production server, not the development server.
Here main:app means 'the object named app inside main.py '. For Flask add gunicorn to requirements.txt, and for FastAPI add fastapi and uvicorn.
Add a health endpoint so the platform and your monitor can check the app is alive:

rows: New Web Service from a GitHub repo
New Project from a GitHub repo
Start command in settings, or a
Persistent disk is a paid add-on
Volumes can be attached to a service

blocks.text: Free-tier behaviour (check current pricing): free web services may sleep when idle and wake slowly on the next request, and their local disk is temporary.
Redeploys. Pushing to the connected branch triggers a new build. After a deploy, open /health first, then test one real request.
Why this matters in practice: the most common first-deploy failure is an app that works locally but the platform reports no open port, because it was bound to localhost or a fixed port.
Real use case: a FastAPI service wrapping your RAG pipeline. A Streamlit front end, or any website, calls its /ask endpoint, and only the service holds the API key.
requirements.txt lists the Python packages the platform must install. If a package is missing, the app crashes with ModuleNotFoundError. If a version changes silently, working code can break.
Pinning means fixing exact versions with ==.

rows: Gets the newest version at build time, which may break your code
Allows small updates, blocks big ones

blocks.text: Pin at least the libraries that change often: LangChain, the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs, Chroma, Streamlit. The version numbers below are examples only. Use the versions you actually tested.

# requirements.txt (example)
streamlit==1.40.0
openai==1.54.0
chromadb==0.5.20
pypdf==5.1.0
python-dotenv==1.0.1
How to produce it

pip freeze > requirements.txt          # exact versions of everything
installed

pip freeze lists everything, including packages you never chose. Many people instead keep a short hand-written list of top-level packages, or use a tool such as pip-tools or uv that creates a lock file.
Test it in a clean environment before you deploy:

python -m venv fresh
source fresh/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
python app.py

Also pin the Python version. Streamlit Cloud has a Python version setting. Render uses the PYTHON_VERSION environment variable. Railway can read a.python-version file or similar settings. Check each platform's docs.

Heavy packages. sentence-transformers installs PyTorch, which is large. It can make builds slow and use more memory than a free plan allows. Options: use a hosted embedding API, choose a CPU-only build, or pick a smaller plan only if you must.
Why this matters in practice: 'it worked yesterday' is often a library that released a new version overnight. Pinned dependencies make builds repeatable.
Real use case: a demo breaks after a redeploy because LangChain moved a class to a new import path. Pinning the version from the working local run fixes it, and you upgrade later on purpose.

15.title: 6. Persisting the vector database across restarts

blocks.text: Most cloud services give your app a temporary filesystem. When the app restarts, redeploys or sleeps, files written at runtime can vanish. A Chroma folder on that disk disappears with it, and your app starts with an empty knowledge base.

rows: Index the documents in the repo when the app boots
Small demos with a few files
Mount a disk and point Chroma at it
Usually one instance only, often paid
Needs a database and some SQL
Repo size, must rebuild when documents change

blocks.text: Example: persistent path from an environment variable, with a safe rebuild

import os
import chromadb

DB_DIR = os.environ.get('VECTOR_DIR', './db')   # on the platform: the disk
mount path, e.g. /data

client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path=DB_DIR)
col = client.get_or_create_collection('docs', metadata={'hnsw:space':
'cosine'})

if col.count() == 0:
    build_index(col)    # your load, chunk, embed, store code from the RAG
notes
The if col.count() == 0 check means a restart with an intact disk skips re-embedding, and a restart with an empty disk rebuilds automatically.
Rules

items: Use stable chunk ids (see RAG Part 1) so re-indexing updates instead of duplicating.
Keep the same embedding model for indexing and querying. If you change it, re- embed everything.
User uploads have the same problem as the index: store them on a volume or in object storage, not on the temporary disk.
Back up what you cannot rebuild.

blocks.text: Real use case: a 'chat with your PDF' app on Render. Without a disk, every redeploy wipes the index. With a mounted disk and VECTOR_DIR=/data, the index survives restarts and only new files are embedded.

15.title: 7. Setting usage limits to prevent runaway cost

blocks.text: A public LLM app is a way for strangers to spend your money. Add limits in layers, because any single layer can fail.

rows: Monthly spend cap and budget alerts
Provider console (check which controls your plan offers)
Step limit, time limit, repeat detection
Requests per day or per minute
Kill switch to disable the model call

blocks.text: Example: simple daily limits

import os
import time
from collections import defaultdict
from fastapi import HTTPException

DAILY_USER_LIMIT = 20
DAILY_TOTAL_TOKENS = 500_000

calls_today = defaultdict(int)
total_tokens = 0
current_day = time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')

def check_limits(user_id):
    global total_tokens, current_day
    if os.environ.get('LLM_DISABLED') == '1':          # kill switch
        raise HTTPException(503, 'Demo is paused.')
    today = time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d')
    if today != current_day:                           # new day: reset
counters
        current_day, total_tokens = today, 0
        calls_today.clear()
    if calls_today[user_id] >= DAILY_USER_LIMIT:
        raise HTTPException(429, 'Daily limit reached. Try again tomorrow.')
    if total_tokens >= DAILY_TOTAL_TOKENS:
        raise HTTPException(503, 'Demo budget for today is used up.')
    calls_today[user_id] += 1
def record_usage(response):
    global total_tokens
    total_tokens += response.usage.total_tokens        # add after each modelcall
Limits of this example: the counters live in memory, so they reset on restart and are not shared between several instances. For a real service, keep them in Redis or a database.
More ways to cut cost (details in the Intro and Agent notes)

items: Use a smaller, cheaper model for easy tasks.
Cache repeated answers and use provider prompt caching for long stable prefixes.
Keep retrieved context short (small k, rerank).
Limit chat history, or summarize it.

blocks.text: Why this matters in practice: the dangerous cases are rare. A bot, a stuck agent loop or one curious user pasting huge documents can cost more than a month of normal use.

Real use case: a public demo has 20 requests per user per day, a 500k daily token cap and a provider budget alert at a small monthly amount. When the cap is hit, the app shows a friendly message instead of calling the model.

15.title: 8. Basic access control on a public demo

blocks.text: A public URL is open to everyone, including bots. Access control decides who may use the app, and it protects both your budget and your data.

rows: Share it only with people you trust
Store codes in a database or secret
Use a library or platform feature, not a homemade scheme
Check what your hosting platform offers
Unwanted calls to an API service

blocks.text: Example: passcode gate in Streamlit

import streamlit as st

if not st.session_state.get('authed'):
    code = st.text_input('Access code', type='password')
    if code and code == get_secret('APP_PASSWORD'):
        st.session_state['authed'] = True
        st.rerun()
    st.stop()          # nothing below this line runs until the code is
correct

# ... the rest of the app ...
Example: access key for a FastAPI service

import hmac
import os
from fastapi import Depends, Header, HTTPException

def require_key(x_demo_key: str = Header(default='')):
    expected = os.environ['DEMO_ACCESS_KEY']
    if not hmac.compare_digest(x_demo_key, expected):   # constant-time
compare
        raise HTTPException(401, 'Invalid access key')

@app.post('/chat', dependencies=[Depends(require_key)])
def chat(req: ChatRequest):
    ...
Rules

items: The passcode and keys come from secrets, never from the code.
Put st.stop() or the dependency before any model call, retrieval or file access.
Combine access control with per-user limits (section 7), so one person cannot use the whole budget.
If the app shows private documents, filter retrieval by user in code (see RAG Part 2). A passcode alone does not separate users.
Restrict CORS on an API service to the origins you actually use.
A shared passcode is a light lock, not strong security. Do not put sensitive data behind it.
Prompt injection still applies: treat documents and web pages as data, and keep tools least-privilege.

blocks.text: Real use case: a portfolio demo shares one passcode with recruiters in the README. If the passcode leaks, you change the secret, redeploy, and the old code stops working.
Logging records what happened. Monitoring watches the logs and metrics and tells you when something is wrong. After deploy you cannot attach a debugger, so logs are how you see the app.
Send logs to standard output. Render, Railway and Streamlit Cloud collect stdout and show it in their log viewer.
What to log for each LLM request

items: Time, request id and a user or session id.
Model name, input tokens, output tokens, latency.
Which chunks were retrieved and their scores (RAG), or which tools were called (agents).
Status: success, error, refused, limit hit, 'I don't know'.

blocks.text: What not to log: API keys, passwords, full documents or personal data. Truncate or hash anything sensitive.
Example: one JSON line per request

import json
import logging
import sys
import time

logging.basicConfig(stream=sys.stdout, level=logging.INFO, format='%
(message)s')
log = logging.getLogger('app')
def log_event(**fields):
    log.info(json.dumps(fields))

start = time.time()
try:
    r = client.chat.completions.create(model='gpt-4o-mini',
messages=messages, max_tokens=300)
    log_event(event='llm_call', user=user_id, model='gpt-4o-mini',
              input_tokens=r.usage.prompt_tokens,
output_tokens=r.usage.completion_tokens,
              latency_ms=int((time.time() - start) * 1000), status='ok')
except Exception as e:
    log_event(event='llm_call', user=user_id, status='error',
error=type(e).__name__)
    raise
One JSON line per event is easy to search and to total up later.
Monitoring basics

rows: An uptime monitor that pings /health every few minutes and alerts you
Watch the platform's log viewer, or a log tool, for error counts
Track latency per request and look at the slowest, not just the average
Add up tokens per day, and set provider budget alerts
Log user feedback (thumbs up or down) and review bad answers

blocks.text: For LLM-specific tracing of chains and agents, tools such as LangSmith can record every step. A plain log is enough to start.
Why this matters in practice: sleeping free apps, quota errors and slow answers all look the same to a user ('it is broken'). Logs tell you which one it is.
Real use case: the daily cost doubles. The logs show one user id making hundreds of calls with very long inputs. You lower the per-user limit and add a maximum input length.

15.title: 10. Reading deploy logs and common failures

blocks.text: A deploy has two phases, and the logs for each look different.
1. Build: the platform installs your dependencies. Failures here mean the app never

items: started.

blocks.text: 2. Run: the platform starts your app. Failures here show as crashes, restarts or a page

items: that never loads.

blocks.text: How to read a log

items: Find the first error, not the last one. Later messages are usually side effects.
Read a Python traceback from the bottom up: the last line names the error, the lines above show where.
Note the phase: was it still installing, or already running?
Compare with what works locally: Python version, package versions, environment variables, file paths.

rows: Add it with a pinned version, redeploy
Build error: no matching version, or conflicting dependencies
A pin that does not exist for this Python, or two packages that disagree
Match the Python version, loosen or fix the conflicting pins
Build fails or is killed while installing
Out of memory or timeout, often from PyTorch or other large packages
Remove heavy packages, use a hosted embedding API
Secret not set on the platform, or misspelled
Add it in the dashboard, check the exact name, redeploy
Create a new key and update the secret
Path works locally only, or the
Works, but the index is empty

blocks.text: Diagnose in order (same idea as the RAG and Agent notes)
1. Did the build finish? If not, it is a dependencies or Python version problem.
2. Did the app start? If not, it is a start command, port or missing-variable problem.
3. Does /health respond? If not, the app crashed or is not reachable.
4. Does a real request work? If not, check the provider error, the secrets and the logs

items: from that request.

blocks.text: Tip: after fixing one problem, redeploy and read the new log from the top. The next error was probably hidden behind the first.
Real use case: a Render deploy shows 'Application failed to respond'. The log shows Uvicorn running on http://127.0.0.1:8000. Changing the start command to bind 0.0.0.0 and $PORT fixes it.

15.title: 11. Writing a README with setup steps, architecture, and screenshots

blocks.text: The README is the front door of your project. Someone who finds your repo should understand it in a minute and run it in ten.
What a good README contains

rows: Title, one-line summary, live demo link
Reader knows what it is and can try it
Shows the result before they read anything
What it can do, in a few bullets
How the pieces connect, as a diagram
Exact commands to run it locally
Where and how you hosted it
Honest about what it does not do
Daily limits, access control, data handling

blocks.text: Screenshots

items: Store images in a docs/ or images/ folder in the repo and link them with a relative path.
Capture the real working app with a meaningful question and answer, not an empty screen.
Check each screenshot for secrets, personal data and private documents before committing.

Real use case: a recruiter opens your repo. In 30 seconds the screenshot and one-line summary tell them what it does, the live link lets them try it, and the architecture section shows you understand the design.

items: No secrets in code, notebooks, README or git history
.env and secrets.toml are in.gitignore
Keys are used only on the server
requirements.txt is pinned and tested in a clean environment
Start command uses 0.0.0.0 and $PORT
/health endpoint responds
Vector DB survives a restart
max_tokens, input limits, per-user and daily limits are set
Provider budget alert is on
Passcode or login protects the demo
Logs show requests, tokens, latency and errors without secrets
README has setup steps, env variable table, architecture and screenshots
Secrets live in environment variables or the platform's secret store, never in code or git. If one leaks, revoke it.
Never ship an API key to the client. Put your own backend between the user and the provider.
Streamlit Community Cloud deploys from GitHub: set the main file, the Python version and the secrets in Advanced settings.
For Flask or FastAPI on Render or Railway, bind to 0.0.0.0 and $PORT, and add a /health route.
Pin dependency versions, pin the Python version, and test the install in a clean environment.
The runtime disk is temporary. Use a volume, a managed vector DB or pgvector, or rebuild the index on start.
Limit cost in layers: provider cap, max_tokens, step limits, per-user limits, a daily total and a kill switch.
A public demo needs at least a passcode. Check access before any model call, and enforce per-user data access in code.
Log one structured line per request to stdout (tokens, latency, status), never secrets, and monitor uptime, errors and spend.
Read deploy logs by phase (build or run), find the first error, and read tracebacks from the bottom.
A good README has a screenshot, an architecture diagram, exact setup steps and an env variable table.

blocks.text: One line to remember: deploy as if strangers will use it and nobody is watching, so keep the keys on the server, put a limit on everything, and leave logs you can read.
